# CT.gov Completion-Delay Debt: Submission-to-Completion Lag Predicts Non-Disclosure Across 216,765 Overdue Interventional Trials

---

## Abstract

**Background:** Non-disclosure in ClinicalTrials.gov has been linked to trial
size, phase, and sponsor class, but the relationship between *submission-to-
completion delay* — the registry-visible operational span of a trial — and its
likelihood of subsequent non-disclosure has not been systematically
characterised.

**Methods:** From the AACT April-12-2026 snapshot we identified 216,765
interventional studies that were closed (COMPLETED/TERMINATED/SUSPENDED/
WITHDRAWN) and whose primary completion date was ≥2 years before the snapshot
(results therefore overdue). Each was assigned a delay bucket = calendar year of
primary completion − calendar year of first registration (same-year, 1, 2, 3–5,
6–10, >10 years). Within each bucket we computed the no-results rate
(`calculated_values.were_results_reported ≠ 't'`) and an independently-computed
ghost-protocol rate (no results **and** no `study_references` row **and** no
`links` row). Treatment-purpose studies (`designs.primary_purpose = TREATMENT`)
formed a pre-specified sub-group.

**Results:** A strict monotonic gradient. Same-year completers: 81.8% no-results,
49.2% ghost (n=45,337). The rate falls with every step of increasing lag: 1-year
72.6%/40.5%, 2-year 67.0%/34.8%, 3–5-year 63.0%/29.6%, 6–10-year 57.6%/24.6%,
>10-year 48.0%/17.1% (n=969). The all-cohort rate was 69.9% no-results, 37.3%
ghost. The identical gradient held within the treatment-purpose sub-group
(same-year 79.4%/48.3% → >10-year 41.9%/14.2%). Same-year completers were
1.42-fold more likely to have no posted results than 6–10-year completers.

**Conclusion:** Fast-cycle studies are the most hidden stratum of the registry.
Operational speed does not translate into reporting speed; short submission-to-
completion lag is a registration-time predictor of eventual silence, likely
reflecting a composition of early-phase, single-arm, and terminated studies with
weaker reporting infrastructure.

---

## 1. Introduction

Registry-based evidence synthesis rests on the assumption that a completed trial
will eventually disclose results. FDAAA 2007 and its 2017 Final Rule mandate
structured results within 12 months of primary completion for applicable trials
[1,2], yet compliance falls well below that standard [3,4], and the *structural*
predictors of non-compliance remain incompletely mapped.

Submission-to-completion delay — the elapsed time between a trial's first
ClinicalTrials.gov registration and its recorded primary completion — is a
registry-visible proxy for operational duration and study type. A study
completed in the same calendar year it was registered is a fundamentally
different object from one enrolling for a decade: the former skews early-phase,
dose-finding, single-arm, or terminated; the latter skews large phase-III
outcome trials with dedicated data-management teams. Whether these operationally
distinct types differ in reporting behaviour — and thus whether lag is a
predictive feature available *at registration, before any result exists* — is
the question here.

---

## 2. Methods

### 2.1 Data source
AACT flat-file export, April-12-2026 ClinicalTrials.gov snapshot. Records were
reassembled by start signature (`^NCT\d{8}\|`) before field splitting because
AACT text fields embed newlines; 59 studies (0.03%) with anomalous field counts
were excluded and reported.

### 2.2 Eligibility
Interventional study type; `overall_status ∈ {COMPLETED, TERMINATED, SUSPENDED,
WITHDRAWN}`; `primary_completion_date ≤ 2024-04-12` (≥2 years before snapshot,
so results are overdue); both first-submission and primary-completion dates
parseable; completion year ≥ submission year (non-negative lag). N = 216,765.

### 2.3 Delay bucket
`year(primary_completion_date) − year(study_first_submitted_date)`, binned into
same-year (0), 1, 2, 3–5, 6–10, >10.

### 2.4 Outcomes
- **No-results rate:** `were_results_reported ≠ 't'` in `calculated_values`
  (studies absent from that table are counted as no-results).
- **Ghost-protocol rate (independent):** no results **and** no row in
  `study_references` **and** no row in `links` (URL-inclusive definition).
- **Treatment sub-group:** `designs.primary_purpose = TREATMENT`.

---

## 3. Results

### 3.1 Complete delay-bucket table (all closed interventional, n = 216,765)

| Delay bucket | n | No-results rate | Ghost-protocol rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Same year | 45,337 | **81.8%** | **49.2%** |
| 1 year | 58,219 | 72.6% | 40.5% |
| 2 years | 42,862 | 67.0% | 34.8% |
| 3–5 years | 56,687 | 63.0% | 29.6% |
| 6–10 years | 12,691 | **57.6%** | 24.6% |
| >10 years | 969 | 48.0% | 17.1% |
| **All** | **216,765** | **69.9%** | **37.3%** |

Both metrics fall **monotonically** with increasing lag — no reversals across
any of the six buckets. Same-year completers are not marginally worse reporters:
the gap to 6–10-year studies is 24.2 pp on no-results and 24.6 pp on ghost
protocols. Fast-cycle studies carry disproportionate silence.

### 3.2 Treatment-purpose sub-group

| Delay bucket | n | No-results rate | Ghost-protocol rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Same year | 24,316 | 79.4% | 48.3% |
| 1 year | 34,917 | 68.4% | 38.8% |
| 2 years | 28,250 | 62.6% | 33.1% |
| 3–5 years | 39,797 | 59.2% | 27.9% |
| 6–10 years | 9,780 | 53.9% | 22.6% |
| >10 years | 762 | 41.9% | 14.2% |

The same monotonic gradient persists in the largest, most clinically salient
sub-group — the effect is **not** an artefact of mixing clinical trials with
administrative or early-phase registrations. Even among treatment trials,
operational speed predicts subsequent silence.

### 3.3 Effect size

Same-year vs 6–10-year no-results: 81.8% / 57.6% = **1.42-fold** higher
non-disclosure for fast-cycle studies (v1 stated "~1.5-fold"; the verified
figure is 1.42×). On ghost protocols the ratio is 49.2% / 24.6% = **2.00-fold**.

### 3.4 Cross-validation with v1
The 6–10-year no-results rate reproduces v1 **exactly** (57.6%), confirming the
methodology matches the original March-snapshot analysis. The same-year rate is
81.8% here vs v1's 85.7%; the difference is attributable to (i) the April vs
March snapshot and (ii) v2's explicit ≥2-year-overdue eligibility window, which
admits more recent same-year completers whose non-disclosure is slightly lower.

---

## 4. Discussion

The lag gradient has a coherent mechanistic reading. Studies completing quickly
relative to registration are disproportionately phase-I safety runs, single-arm
studies, or trials terminated before planned completion — study types that
frequently have no structured results to post and lack dedicated reporting
infrastructure. Long-lag studies (6–10 years) are enriched for large funded
phase-III outcome trials, the very features associated with better FDAAA
compliance in cross-disease audits [3,4].

Two implications follow. **For policy:** the uniform 12-month post-completion
clock operates very differently across operational-duration strata. For
same-year completers the clock runs against studies that may have terminated
without usable results or registered late relative to actual start; the
instrument may need to distinguish these cases. **For systematic reviewers:** a
trial that completed in its registration year is 1.42-fold more likely to have
no posted results (and twice as likely to be a full ghost) than a long-lag
trial — a risk factor visible at search time, absent from most review protocols,
and worth incorporating into trial-level completeness assessments and
selective-reporting risk-of-bias judgements [10].

The ghost-protocol rate (no results, no reference, no link) is the stricter
signal: it identifies trials that are not merely unreported but effectively
invisible to a reader trying to reach *any* fuller account. That 49.2% of
same-year completers meet this bar is the paper's sharpest finding.

---

## 5. Limitations

Submission-to-completion delay is a registry proxy for operational duration; it
does not capture enrolment start, unblinding, or reporting intent, and
retroactive registration inflates the same-year bucket with trials whose "true"
span was longer. Calendar-year bucketing (rather than exact months) introduces
grouping artefacts at bucket edges. The ghost-protocol definition is
URL-inclusive and should not be compared to non-URL-inclusive figures elsewhere.
Registry-visible absence establishes neither intent nor culpability. Studies
absent from `calculated_values` are treated as no-results, a conservative choice
that could slightly overstate non-disclosure in any bucket uniformly.

---

## 6. Conclusion

Across 216,765 overdue closed interventional ClinicalTrials.gov studies,
non-disclosure falls monotonically with submission-to-completion lag: same-year
completers show 81.8% no-results and 49.2% ghost protocols; >10-year studies
fall to 48.0% and 17.1%. The gradient persists within treatment-purpose trials.
Fast-cycle studies are the most hidden stratum of the registry — operational
speed does not translate into reporting speed — and short lag is a
registration-time predictor of eventual silence.
